the-three-steps.question: A measurement says “when x = 6.” When do you use that 6 in the rate calculation?
the-three-steps.hint: Which equations describe the entire motion, and which values describe one instant?
choices: Differentiate the relation, then evaluate at x = 6.
feedback: That would treat x as constant and erase its rate. The measurement specifies one instant.
Yes. Keep x(t) variable while differentiating. Then use x(t₀) = 6 in the equation relating the rates.
The 6 is a position. A rate would have units of position per unit of time.

help.question: How do I tell which rate I know and which one to find?
help.explanation: Underline the quantity next to “per second” or “per minute.” For the balloon, cubic centimeters per second describe volume, so the given rate is \(dV/dt\). The question asks how fast its radius grows, so the unknown is \(dr/dt\). Make those two labels on your own sketch.

the-three-steps.starter: Draw the situation at a general time \(t\). Label the quantities that change and identify the rate you know and the rate you want.

answers.question: When can I use the measurements in my equation?
answers.text: Ask whether the number would still be true a second later. A rigid 10-ft ladder stays 10 ft long, so its length can go into the starting equation. Its foot passes \(x=6\) at just one instant. Differentiate with \(x(t)\) still variable, then use \(x=6\).

parabola.question: On y = x², which derivative tells you how fast y changes with time?
parabola.hint: The point moves, so x itself depends on time.
feedback: 2x is dy/dx. Convert change per unit of x to change per unit of time.
Squaring the rate does not differentiate the square of a moving coordinate. Apply the chain rule.
Yes. The factor dx/dt accounts for how fast the point moves horizontally.

help.question: I found the slope. How do I turn it into a rate over time?
help.explanation: At \(x=3\), the slope \(dy/dx=2x=6\) measures vertical change per unit of horizontal change. The point travels horizontally at \(dx/dt=2\) units per unit time. Multiply the two rates to obtain \(dy/dt\). Which units cancel?

reply.text: The horizontal units cancel in \((dy/dx)(dx/dt)\). What remains is vertical change per unit time, and here \(dy/dt=6(2)=12\).

parabola.starter: Write \(y(t)=x(t)^2\). Differentiate both sides with respect to time before using \(x=3\). Which factor records how fast \(x\) changes?

answers.question: Why do I keep x variable when the point is at x = 3?
answers.text: At this instant \(x=3\), but the point keeps moving. Writing \(y=9\) before differentiating loses that motion. Start from \(y(t)=x(t)^2\) and put 3 into the rate equation afterward.

constant-product.question: The point moves while xy = 12. Which equation relates its two rates?
constant-product.hint: Both factors can change even though their product stays fixed.
feedback: Yes. The two product-rule terms add to zero because the derivative of 12 is zero.
Differentiate a product by changing one factor at a time and adding the two contributions.
Both factors vary. The derivative of the fixed right-hand side is zero.

help.question: If xy stays at 12, how can either coordinate change?
help.explanation: Imagine increasing \(x\) from 3 to 4. To keep \(xy=12\), \(y\) must drop from 4 to 3. The rate equation expresses that balance. \(y\,dx/dt+x\,dy/dt=0\). If \(dy/dt<0\) at \((3,4)\), what sign must \(dx/dt\) have?

reply.text: At \((3,4)\), the term \(x\,dy/dt\) is negative. To balance it, \(y\,dx/dt\) must be positive, so \(dx/dt>0\).

constant-product.starter: Write \(x(t)y(t)=12\). Both factors change. What two terms do you get when you differentiate their product?

answers.question: Why do I add two terms when I differentiate xy?
answers.text: Changing \(x\) contributes \(y\,dx/dt\). Changing \(y\) contributes \(x\,dy/dt\). Add both contributions. Because the product stays at 12, their sum must equal zero. Try putting the given negative rate into the second term.

circle.question: The point (3, 4) moves to the right on x² + y² = 25. What sign should dy/dt have?
circle.hint: In the first quadrant, what must happen to y if x increases and the radius stays fixed?
feedback: Increasing both coordinates would increase x² + y².
Yes. Near (3, 4), increasing x forces y to decrease along the fixed circle.
The radius stays fixed. The vertical coordinate changes as the point moves right.

help.question: Can I predict whether y goes up or down before calculating?
help.explanation: Put your pencil at \((3,4)\) and trace the circle a little to the right. Its radius stays fixed. As \(x^2\) grows, \(y^2\) must shrink to keep \(x^2+y^2=25\). Here \(y>0\), so the vertical rate is negative.

circle.starter: Start with \(x^2+y^2=25\). The radius is fixed as the point moves. Differentiate both sides with respect to \(t\) before using the point \((3,4)\).

answers.question: Why is there a zero on the right of the rate equation?
answers.text: The right side of \(x^2+y^2=25\) is the square of a fixed radius. Its time derivative is zero. Both coordinates can still move: \(2x\,dx/dt+2y\,dy/dt=0\). Which term must offset the positive horizontal contribution?

cube.question: The cube loses 12 m³ of volume per second. Which rate is given?
cube.hint: Read the units, then decide whether the quantity is increasing or decreasing.
feedback: Cubic meters measure volume. The side-length rate is the unknown.
The units are right. Losing volume makes its signed rate negative.
Yes. Start with this signed volume rate and differentiate V = s³ to relate it to ds/dt.

help.question: The cube loses volume. How do I find the rate for one edge?
help.explanation: The units \(\mathrm{m^3/s}\) identify a volume rate, and “loses” gives \(dV/dt=-12\). Let \(s\) be one edge. From \(V=s^3\) you get \(dV/dt=3s^2\,ds/dt\). Put \(s=2\) into that equation and isolate the edge rate.

cube.starter: Let \(s\) be the edge length. Write \(V=s^3\). The given rate describes a loss of volume. What sign should \(dV/dt\) have?

answers.question: Why does the edge rate have different units from the volume rate?
answers.text: An edge is a length, so \(ds/dt\) is measured in \(\mathrm{m/s}\). The factor \(3s^2\) has units of square meters. Check that multiplying the two gives the stated volume units per second.

cube.teaching_note: At s=2 m the divisor 3s² equals 12 square meters. Dividing -12 cubic meters per second by 12 square meters gives -1 meter per second.

balloon.question: Air enters at 12π cm³/s. What units should the answer for dr/dt have?
balloon.hint: The requested quantity is a radius.
feedback: Yes. A radius is a length. In dV/dt = 4πr² · dr/dt, area times length per second gives volume per second.
Square centimeters per second would describe a changing area.
These are the units of the given volume rate. The requested rate describes a length.

help.question: Does the incoming air tell me the radius rate or the volume rate?
help.explanation: Each second the balloon gains \(12\pi\) cubic centimeters of air. That gives \(dV/dt\). To turn this into a radius rate, divide by the surface area to get \(dr/dt=(dV/dt)/(4\pi r^2)\). Use the radius at the requested instant. What units are left?

reply.text: Dividing \(\mathrm{cm^3/s}\) by \(\mathrm{cm^2}\) leaves \(\mathrm{cm/s}\), the units of a radius rate. At \(r=2\), the area is \(16\pi\,\mathrm{cm^2}\). Divide the incoming \(12\pi\) by that area.

balloon.starter: The air entering gives \(dV/dt\), while the question asks for \(dr/dt\). Start with \(V=\tfrac43\pi r^3\). How can you relate the two rates?

answers.question: Why does surface area appear in the radius calculation?
answers.text: Picture a thin new layer of air covering the whole balloon. Its volume is approximately its surface area times its thickness. In the limit this gives \(dV/dt=4\pi r^2\,dr/dt\). At a larger radius, the same inflow spreads over more area.

balloon.teaching_note: The volume grows by the same amount each second. The same extra volume spreads across a larger surface, producing a thinner shell. At fixed flow, doubling radius quadruples surface area and quarters radial speed. The volume growth rate stays constant.

rectangle.question: If the length grows while the width shrinks, which expression decides whether the area increases?
rectangle.hint: Differentiate A = LW and track the sign of each contribution.
feedback: The derivative of a product has two additive terms. Multiplying the rates also gives the wrong time units.
Yes. The first term measures the gain from the length. The second is negative as the width shrinks.
These terms each measure length per second. The dimensions L and W convert them to area per second.

help.question: Why are there two terms when I differentiate the area?
help.explanation: Picture the changing edges. The length adds a strip spanning the width, at \(W\,dL/dt\). The shrinking width removes a strip along the length, at \(L\,dW/dt\). Adding the signed contributions gives \(dA/dt=W\,dL/dt+L\,dW/dt\). Which term is negative here?

reply.text: The width is shrinking, so \(dW/dt=-1\). It appears in the second term, \(L\,dW/dt=8(-1)\). The length is growing and contributes \(W\,dL/dt=5(3)\). Compare the 15 square centimeters gained each second with the 8 lost.

rectangle.starter: The rectangle is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide at this instant. Its length grows at \(3\,\mathrm{cm/s}\), and its width shrinks at \(1\,\mathrm{cm/s}\), so \(dW/dt=-1\). We want the area rate \(dA/dt\). What equation connects the area \(A\) to the length \(L\) and width \(W\)?

answers.text: \(8\cdot5=40\,\mathrm{cm^2}\) gives the area at this instant. The question asks how many square centimeters the area gains each second. Keep the dimensions variable in \(A(t)=L(t)W(t)\), then differentiate with respect to time.

answers.match: \ba\s*=\s*(?:l\s*\+\s*w|w\s*\+\s*l)\b|(?:length plus width|add the length and width)
answers.text: Adding length and width gives a length in centimeters. Area has square centimeters as its units. Multiplying the two side lengths gives \(A=LW\). Keep both sides variable as you take the time derivative.

Use \(A=LW\). Both dimensions change, so the product rule gives \(dA/dt=W\,dL/dt+L\,dW/dt\). The first term accounts for the growing length, the second for the shrinking width. Substitute the signed rates to get \(5(3)+8(-1)\). What area rate does that give?

reply.text: The growing length adds \(5(3)=15\) square centimeters per second. The shrinking width removes \(8(1)=8\). Their net contribution is \(dA/dt=15-8=7\,\mathrm{cm^2/s}\), so at that instant the area is increasing.

answers.match: ^(?:i (?:get|got)|is it|so|the area rate is)?\s*[+−-]?(?:7|23)(?:\s*(?:cm(?:\^?2|²)|square centimet(?:er|re)s?)(?:\s*/\s*s(?:ec(?:ond)?)?| per second)?)?\s*(?:right|is that right)?$|\b15\s*[-−]\s*8\s*=\s*7\b
answers.text: The growing length adds \(5(3)=15\) square centimeters per second. The shrinking width removes \(8(1)=8\). Their net contribution is \(dA/dt=15-8=7\,\mathrm{cm^2/s}\), so at that instant the area is increasing.

answers.question: Can the area increase while the width gets smaller?
answers.text: The growing length adds \(5(3)=15\) square centimeters each second. The shrinking width contributes \(8(-1)=-8\) in the same units. Add the two signed changes and use the sign to describe the area.

rectangle.teaching_note: Length and width rates sum to d(L+W)/dt = 2 cm/s, half the perimeter rate. The perimeter grows at 4 cm/s. The area gains 15 and loses 8 square centimeters per second. Each centimeter of new length adds a strip as wide as the rectangle (5 cm).

triangle.question: The base and height of the triangle both change. Why does a factor of one-half remain in the area rate?
triangle.hint: Start with the area formula before applying the product rule.
choices: Only one of the two lengths changes at an instant.
The derivatives of the base and height are equal.
The area is one-half of base times height at every instant.
feedback: The base and height change simultaneously. The product rule includes both rates.
The lecture gives different signed rates for the base and height. The one-half comes from geometry.
Yes. A = ½bh throughout the motion. Its constant factor multiplies both product-rule terms.

help.question: How do I keep track of the shrinking base and growing height?
help.explanation: Label the sketch with \(db/dt=-2\) and \(dh/dt=3\) cm/min. In \(dA/dt=\tfrac12(h\,db/dt+b\,dh/dt)\), the first term measures what the shrinking base removes. Which term measures what the height adds?

reply.text: The growing height contributes \(\tfrac12 b\,dh/dt=\tfrac12(8)(3)\). The shrinking base contributes \(\tfrac12 h\,db/dt=\tfrac12(6)(-2)\). Add them to find the net area change.

triangle.starter: Write \(A=\tfrac12 bh\). The base and height both change. Keep both variable as you differentiate, and leave the factor \(\tfrac12\) in front.

answers.question: Where does the one-half go when I use the product rule?
answers.text: The triangle occupies half the area of a rectangle with the same base and height. So the constant \(\tfrac12\) multiplies the entire derivative of \(bh\). Put parentheses around both product-rule terms before multiplying by \(\tfrac12\).

ladder.question: The foot of the ladder is 6 ft from the wall at one instant. Which quantity can you replace with a number before differentiating?
ladder.hint: Picture the ladder a moment later. Which length must still be the same?
feedback: Yes. The ladder stays 10 ft long throughout the motion, so x² + y² = 100. Keep x and y variable until after differentiating.
The foot is moving. Writing x = 6 for the whole motion would incorrectly give dx/dt = 0.
The top is sliding. Its height is 8 ft only when the foot is 6 ft from the wall.

help.question: How do I turn the ladder sketch into a rate equation?
help.explanation: The foot’s distance \(x\) and the top’s height \(y\) are the legs of a right triangle. The ladder stays 10 ft long, so \(x^2+y^2=100\). Differentiate in time and divide by 2 to get \(x\,dx/dt+y\,dy/dt=0\). To find the top’s rate, which term would you move across the equals sign?

reply.text: Move the horizontal term to obtain \(y\,dy/dt=-x\,dx/dt\). Divide by \(y\), then put in \(x=6\), \(y=8\), and \(dx/dt=2\) for part (a).

ladder.starter: Let \(x\) be the distance of the foot from the wall and \(y\) the height of the top. The ladder is the fixed hypotenuse. What equation relates \(x\), \(y\), and 10?

partHints.a: The foot moves away from the wall, so \(dx/dt>0\). Differentiate the fixed-length equation. Which rate describes the top?
partHints.b: The top moves downward, so \(dy/dt=-3\) ft/s. Use the same differentiated equation as in part (a), this time solving for \(dx/dt\).

answers.text: The fixed hypotenuse gives \(x^2+y^2=10^2\). Differentiate both changing legs in time. You should get \(2x\,dx/dt+2y\,dy/dt=0\). Which rate describes the end of the ladder you are tracking?

The 10-ft ladder keeps its length throughout the motion. The foot is 6 ft from the wall at only one instant. If you set \(x=6\) in the starting equation, its derivative becomes zero. Keep \(x(t)\) until you have the rate equation.

answers.question: I got a positive speed. What sign should the height rate have?
answers.text: In part (a), watch the top as the foot slides out. Its height falls. In the rate equation \(dy/dt=-(x/y)\,dx/dt\), the quotient and the horizontal rate are both positive. Report \(dy/dt=-1.5\,\mathrm{ft/s}\), or a speed of \(1.5\,\mathrm{ft/s}\) downward.

partNudges.a: Use \(x\,dx/dt+y\,dy/dt=0\). Move the horizontal term across the equals sign before dividing by \(y\). What sign should the top’s rate have?
partNudges.b: The known rate is now \(dy/dt=-3\) ft/s. Start from \(x\,dx/dt=-y\,dy/dt\). Which length will you divide by to get the foot’s rate?

ladder.teaching_note: For a learner asking only to start, invite them to label the two moving legs and the fixed 10-ft hypotenuse and write their relation. Stop there so the student can try before differentiating.

boat.question: Which rate equals −1 m/s when the rope is pulled in at 1 m/s?
boat.hint: Use L for the taut rope and x for the horizontal distance.
choices: The rate of change of the 3-m vertical separation
feedback: The boat’s horizontal speed is the quantity to find. The given speed describes the rope.
Yes. The taut rope shortens. Use its negative rate in L · dL/dt = x · dx/dt.
The vertical separation stays fixed, so its rate of change is zero.

help.question: Why is pulling in rope different from moving the boat toward the dock?
help.explanation: The rope runs diagonally from boat to pulley. Its length \(L\) and the horizontal gap \(x\) are different sides of a triangle with fixed height 3 m. Differentiate \(L^2=x^2+3^2\) to get \(L\,dL/dt=x\,dx/dt\). Which derivative does the winch give you?

reply.text: The winch shortens the diagonal rope, giving \(dL/dt=-1\,\mathrm{m/s}\). At a horizontal distance of 4 m the rope is 5 m long. Use those lengths to solve for \(dx/dt\).

boat.starter: Draw the right triangle from the pulley to the boat. Label the rope \(L\), the horizontal distance \(x\), and the fixed vertical side 3 m. Which length is getting shorter?

answers.question: Should the rope rate be positive or negative as I pull it in?
answers.text: Imagine marking the taut length at two times one second apart. It is 1 m shorter the second time, so \(dL/dt=-1\,\mathrm{m/s}\). The horizontal gap also shrinks. Use that observation to check the sign of \(dx/dt\).

boat.teaching_note: The vertical gap is constant throughout. The horizontal motion changes only the rope component parallel to its own length: dL/dt = (x/L) dx/dt. Because 0 < x/L < 1, the horizontal distance changes more than the rope length, also over any finite pull while the rope stays taut and the gap positive. At x=4 and L=5, the signed rates are -1 m/s for rope and -1.25 m/s for the boat. The instantaneous factor 5/4 varies over a finite pull.

similar-triangles.question: The small triangle has sides a, b, c corresponding to A, B, C. What is the scaling factor from the large triangle to the small one?
similar-triangles.hint: Multiplying the large side A by the factor must give a.
feedback: This scales the small side up to the large side. Check the direction in the question.
Match corresponding sides. Here a corresponds to A.
Yes. Multiplying A by a/A gives a. The same ratio equals b/B and c/C.

help.question: How do I pair the sides before writing a proportion?
help.explanation: Match equal angles first. The sides opposite them correspond. If \(a\) is opposite the same angle as \(A\), write \(a/A\), then use the same small-over-large order for \(b/B\) and \(c/C\).

similar-triangles.starter: Match the corresponding sides, starting with \(a\) in the small triangle and \(A\) in the large triangle. Which factor takes \(A\) to \(a\)?

answers.question: How can I check whether I flipped the scaling factor?
answers.text: Try multiplying a starting side by your factor. To go from large side \(A\) to small side \(a\), the product must be \(a\). Since \(A(a/A)=a\), the large-to-small factor is \(a/A\). It should be less than 1.

cone.question: In the 6-m tank of radius 2 m, which relation stays true as the water rises?
cone.hint: Compare radius to height in an axial cross section of the water and of the whole tank.
feedback: Yes. Similar triangles give the same radius-to-height ratio, so r = h/3 at every depth.
2 m is the radius of the full tank. The water-surface radius changes with the depth.
Use the same order for both triangles. The left side is radius divided by height.

help.question: How do I write the water volume using only its depth?
help.explanation: The cone formula \(V=\tfrac13\pi r^2h\) still has two changing lengths. In a vertical slice the water cone and tank have the same shape, so \(r/h=2/6\) and \(r=h/3\). Replace \(r\) by \(h/3\) in the volume formula. What happens to the 3 when you square that radius?

reply.text: Squaring the denominator gives \(3\cdot3=9\), so \((h/3)^2=h^2/9\). The cone formula supplies one more factor of \(1/3\), giving \(V=\pi h^3/27\).

cone.starter: Draw a vertical slice through the tip of the tank. Label the water depth \(h\) and surface radius \(r\). The full tank has radius 2 m and height 6 m. What ratio of corresponding sides relates \(r\) and \(h\)?

partHints.a: Draw a vertical slice through the tip of the tank. Label the water depth \(h\) and surface radius \(r\). The full tank has radius 2 m and height 6 m. What ratio of corresponding sides relates \(r\) and \(h\)?
partHints.b: Use your volume formula \(V(h)\). Differentiate with respect to time, then use \(h=3\) and the known inflow \(dV/dt=\pi\). What rate remains unknown?
partHints.c: The tank has the same shape and the water is at the same depth. Draining reverses the sign of \(dV/dt\). What should happen to the sign of \(dh/dt\)?

answers.text: \(dh/dt\) is the rate the problem asks for. It measures the change in water depth in meters per minute. From \(V=\pi h^3/27\), differentiate to get \(dV/dt=(\pi h^2/9)\,dh/dt\). At \(h=3\), divide the given volume rate by \(\pi\) to obtain the depth rate.

Try that equation on the full tank. At \(h=6\), the rule \(r=3h\) would predict an 18-m radius. The actual radius is 2 m. Putting radius first in both fractions gives \(r/h=2/6\). What radius does the repaired ratio give at \(h=3\)?

reply.text: At \(h=3\) m, \(r=h/3=1\) m. Your sketch now passes that check. Use the variable expression \(h/3\) for the radius when you build \(V(h)\).

answers.text: The ratio \(r/h=2/6\), or equivalently \(h/r=6/2\), gives the tank’s 2-m radius when \(h=6\). Use \(r=h/3\) in \(V=\tfrac13\pi r^2h\). Remember to square the whole fraction.
Both the numerator and denominator are squared: \((h/3)^2=h^2/9\). Now multiply by the remaining \(h\) and the cone’s factor \(\pi/3\). This gives \(V=\pi h^3/27\).

answers.question: How do I check if my radius-to-depth ratio is upside down?
answers.text: Test the ratio when the tank is full. Its radius is 2 m and its depth is 6 m. Radius over depth must give \(r/h=2/6=1/3\). Reversing both sides gives \(h/r=6/2=3\). At a depth of 3 m your relation should predict a radius of 1 m.

\(dV/dt\) tells you how many cubic meters of water enter or leave each minute. In part (b) it is \(+\pi\;\mathrm{m^3/min}\); in part (c) it is \(-\pi\;\mathrm{m^3/min}\). The rate you want is \(dh/dt\), the change in depth.
When water drains, \(dV/dt<0\). At the same depth the water-surface area is still positive, so \(dh/dt\) also becomes negative. The minus sign records the falling water level.
When \(h=3\,\mathrm m\), the rate equation is \(dV/dt=\pi\,dh/dt\). The tank fills at \(\pi\,\mathrm{m^3/min}\), so the water level rises at \(1\,\mathrm{m/min}\).

partNudges.a: Start with \(r/h\) on the water triangle. Write the same two sides, in that order, on the full tank. Once you have \(r\) in terms of \(h\), which letter can you replace in the volume formula?
partNudges.b: From \(V=\pi h^3/27\), differentiate the cube by the chain rule. The factor next to \(dh/dt\) should contain \(h^2\). Try evaluating just that factor at \(h=3\).
partNudges.c: Write the rate equation for part (b) again. The depth is still \(h=3\), so its coefficient is the same. Look at the sign of the volume rate when water leaves.

cone.teaching_note: Corresponding horizontal and vertical sides give r/h = 2/6. Turning a diagram upside down preserves the ratio. The reciprocal equation is h/r = 6/2. Compare the proposed and actual radius numerically when a learner asks about their own proportion: at h=3, r=3h gives 9 m whereas r=h/3 gives 1 m. The entire tank has radius only 2 m.

shadow.question: Let x be the distance from light to person and s the shadow length. Which rate measures motion of the shadow tip away from the light?
shadow.hint: Write the distance from the light to the tip before differentiating.
feedback: This is the change in shadow length measured from the moving person. Include the person’s distance from the light.
Yes. The distance from the light to the tip is x + s. Both terms change as the person walks.
This is the person’s walking rate. The shadow tip lies beyond the person.

help.question: Which distance am I measuring when I track the shadow tip?
help.explanation: Mark the lamp, the person, and the tip in that order. From the lamp to the person is \(x\). From the person to the tip is \(s\). The tip is \(x+s\) from the lamp, so its rate includes both \(dx/dt\) and \(ds/dt\). Which distance does part (a) ask for?

reply.text: Part (a) measures the length \(s\) from the person to the tip. The similar triangles give \(s=x/2\), so its rate is half the walking rate. For part (b), take the lamp as your starting point.

shadow.starter: Draw the triangle from the lamp to the shadow tip. If \(x\) is the lamp-to-person distance and \(s\) is the shadow length, what is the base of the large triangle?

partHints.a: Use similar triangles to relate \(s\) to \(x\). The question asks for the rate of the shadow length, \(ds/dt\).
partHints.b: The tip is \(x+s\) from the lamp. Which two rates contribute to the speed of the tip?

answers.question: I got 1 m/s. Is that the shadow length rate or the tip speed?
answers.text: The shadow length is \(s=x/2\), so \(ds/dt=1\,\mathrm{m/s}\). That is the rate measured from the moving person. For the tip measured from the lamp, add the person’s \(2\,\mathrm{m/s}\) to the length rate.
The tip is \(x+s\) from the light. The person walks at \(dx/dt=2\,\mathrm{m/s}\) and the shadow length grows at \(ds/dt=1\,\mathrm{m/s}\), so the tip moves at \(3\,\mathrm{m/s}\).

partNudges.a: Compare height to base in each triangle: \(6/(x+s)=2/s\). Cross-multiply and collect the terms in \(s\) before differentiating.
partNudges.b: Mark the distance \(x+s\) from the stationary lamp to the tip. Differentiate that sum and identify the walking rate and the length rate separately.

shadow.teaching_note: The shadow length runs from the walker to the tip. Its growth rate is 1 m/s. The distance measured FROM THE LIGHT runs from the lamp to the tip, x+s, and grows at 3 m/s. A measurement of length alone in meters never determines a rate in meters per second.
